pos: n. pl. (the covenant people of Judah; Hebrew Yehudim, Greek Ioudaioi)
etymology: From Judah, the tribe and kingdom that survived the Assyrian deportation. After the captivity the name of one tribe became the name of the whole remnant.
biblical_def: Jews is the post-exilic name of the covenant people, taken from Judah and spread over the whole surviving nation. It is a name born in exile: when the northern tribes were scattered and Judah alone carried the promise, the part gave its name to the whole. Scripture never treats the term as merely ethnic. To be a Jew is to stand inside the covenant of Abraham, to be entrusted with the oracles of God, and to be marked in the flesh by circumcision. Our Lord, Himself a Jew after the flesh, tells the woman of Samaria that “salvation is of the Jews” (Joh 4:22) — not that the Jews save, but that the Saviour comes out from them, according to promise. Paul asks the plain question, “What advantage then hath the Jew?” and answers it at length: much every way, chiefly that unto them were committed the oracles of God. The gospel itself keeps this order, going “to the Jew first, and also to the Greek” (Rom 1:16). Yet the same apostle insists that he is not a Jew who is one outwardly. The name honours a real lineage and a real deposit of revelation, and it summons the one who bears it to the circumcision of the heart which the outward sign always signified.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Jew as a Hebrew or Israelite, the name derived from Judah.
webster_full: JEW, n. [from Judah.] A Hebrew or Israelite.
JEWESS, n. A Hebrew woman.
JEWISH, a. Pertaining to the Jews or Hebrews.
JEWRY, n. Judea; also, a district inhabited by Jews.
The name Jew came into general use after the captivity, when the tribe of Judah formed the chief part of the returning remnant.
scriptures: Est 8:17

And in every province, and in every city, whithersoever the king's commandment and his decree came, the Jews had joy and gladness, a feast and a good day. And many of the people of the land became Jews; for the fear of the Jews fell upon them.
Joh 4:22
Ye worship ye know not what: we know what we worship: for salvation is of the Jews.
Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
Rom 3:1
What advantage then hath the Jew? or what profit is there of circumcision?
corruption_summary: The name is bent two ways at once — into a slur by the hater, and into a merely ethnic label by those who wish the covenant emptied of its promises.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors press on this word from opposite sides. The first is the ancient malice that has made Jew a term of contempt, a thing Scripture forbids twice over: God has not cast away His people whom He foreknew, and the branches grafted in are warned expressly not to boast against the natural branches. The second is subtler and now more common — the reduction of the name to bare ethnicity, a heritage with no oracles in it, so that the covenant becomes a culture and the promises become sentiment. Paul will allow neither. He magnifies the advantage, then presses the circumcision of the heart.

The recovery is to read the word as the apostle reads it: a real people, a real lineage, a real deposit of revelation, and a real summons. “Salvation is of the Jews” is a statement about Christ's descent, not about any man's standing before God apart from Him. The believing Gentile owes the Jew the debt of the oracles and the Messiah; the Jew, like every son of Adam, is saved only by that Messiah. Honour the lineage, preach the Christ who came of it, and let no contempt and no flattery displace the gospel that goes to the Jew first.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yehudi (H3064), a man of Judah; from Yehudah (H3063), Judah, ‘praise’; Greek Ioudaios (G2453).
roots_lines: Hebrew Yehudi (H3064) — a Jew, man of Judah; Esther 2:5, Jeremiah 34:9, Zechariah 8:23.
Hebrew Yehudah (H3063) — Judah, from yadah, to praise or give thanks; Genesis 29:35.
Greek Ioudaios (G2453) — a Jew, Judean; John 4:22, Romans 1:16, Romans 2:28-29.
Greek Ioudaismos (G2454) — the Jews' religion; Galatians 1:13-14.
The name spread from one tribe to the whole remnant after the Babylonian captivity.
usage: “Salvation is of the Jews” — the Saviour's lineage, not any man's merit.
“To the Jew first, and also to the Greek” — the gospel's appointed order.
“Many of the people of the land became Jews” — Esther's deliverance drew proselytes.

pos: n. pl. (the tribe of Levi set apart for sanctuary service; Hebrew Lewiyyim)
etymology: From Levi, third son of Jacob and Leah. The tribe that had been scattered in Jacob's prophecy was scattered indeed — but into the service of God.
biblical_def: The Levites are the tribe of Levi, taken by God out of Israel and given to Aaron for the work of the tabernacle. Their claim rests on a substitution: the LORD had sanctified every firstborn in Israel to Himself in the night of the passover, and He then took the Levites “instead of all the firstborn” (Num 3:12), so that the whole tribe stands in the room of a nation's eldest sons. They bore the ark, they camped around the tabernacle as a living fence between the holy things and the congregation, they taught the law, and they blessed in the LORD's name. They received no territorial inheritance; the tenth in Israel was given them instead, and the LORD Himself was called their portion. Jacob had prophesied that Levi would be divided in Jacob and scattered in Israel — a word spoken in rebuke for the violence at Shechem, yet fulfilled in mercy, for the scattering became forty-eight cities of instruction sown through every tribe. The order is typical throughout: a people substituted, a service assigned, an inheritance that is God Himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Levite as one of the tribe of Levi, appointed to the lower offices of the sanctuary.
webster_full: LEVITE, n. One of the tribe or family of Levi; a descendant of Levi.
2. One of that tribe employed in the lower services of the temple, as distinguished from the priests.
LEVITICAL, a. Belonging to the Levites, or to the tribe of Levi.
LEVITICUS, n. The third book of Moses, containing the laws of the priesthood and sacrifices.
The Levites had no inheritance of land, but received the tithes of the other tribes.
scriptures: Num 3:12
And I, behold, I have taken the Levites from among the children of Israel instead of all the firstborn that openeth the matrix among the children of Israel: therefore the Levites shall be mine;
Num 8:14
Thus shalt thou separate the Levites from among the children of Israel: and the Levites shall be mine.
Deu 10:8
At that time the LORD separated the tribe of Levi, to bear the ark of the covenant of the LORD, to stand before the LORD to minister unto him, and to bless in his name, unto this day.
And, behold, I have given the children of Levi all the tenth in Israel for an inheritance, for their service which they serve, even the service of the tabernacle of the congregation.
corruption_summary: Set-apart service is read as clerical privilege, when Scripture presents it as substitution, labour, and the surrender of an inheritance.
corruption_paragraphs: The Levite is often imagined as a man of leisure kept by other men's tithes — a caste enjoying religion at the nation's expense. The text says the reverse. The Levites carried the tabernacle on their shoulders, guarded its vessels on pain of death, and were forbidden the one thing every other Israelite received: land. The tenth was not a salary but the substitute for an inheritance, and it came with the charge that they themselves tithe of the tithe. Their honour and their loss were the same fact.

The recovery is to see the whole tribe as a standing type. They were taken instead of the firstborn, which is the logic of substitution written into the census; they had no portion, which is the logic of the minister who lives by the altar; and they blessed in the LORD's name, which is the logic of a mediated word. All of it points forward to the one Levite's better than Levi, the Priest after the order of Melchisedec, and to a people made kings and priests who likewise hold their true inheritance in God and not in ground.
roots_lines: Hebrew Lewi (H3878) — Levi, from lawah, to join; Genesis 29:34.
Hebrew Lewiyyi (H3881) — a Levite; Numbers 3:12, Deuteronomy 10:8.
Hebrew maaser (H4643) — a tenth, the tithe given the Levites; Numbers 18:21.
Greek Leuites (G3019) — a Levite; Luke 10:32, John 1:19, Acts 4:36.
Jacob's word that Levi would be scattered (Genesis 49:7) was fulfilled in forty-eight Levitical cities.
usage: “The Levites shall be mine” — a tribe taken in the room of the firstborn.
“To bear the ark… to stand… to bless” — the threefold Levitical charge.
“I have given the children of Levi all the tenth” — the tithe instead of a territory.

pos: n. pl. (Hellenes; in the New Testament often the Gentile world at large; Greek Hellenes)
etymology: From Hellen, the reputed father of the Hellenic race. In apostolic usage the national name widens into a category: everyone who is not a Jew.
biblical_def: Greeks in the New Testament rarely means only the inhabitants of Greece. Paired against Jew, it stands for the whole Gentile world — the nations outside the covenant, characterised by their appetite for wisdom as the Jews were characterised by their demand for a sign. Some Greeks were devout worshippers who came up to the feast and asked, “Sir, we would see Jesus.” Others filled the synagogues of the dispersion as God-fearers and became the first harvest of Paul's preaching. The apostle's great antitheses turn on the word: the gospel is to the Jew first and also to the Greek; the Jews require a sign and the Greeks seek after wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, to the Greeks foolishness; and in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek. That last word abolishes not the nations but the wall between them. The Greek is not made a Jew, nor the Jew a Greek; both are made one new man, and the wisdom the Greek sought is found where he would never have looked for it — in a cross.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Greek as a native of Greece, and notes the language in which the New Testament was written.
webster_full: GREEK, n. A native of Greece; also, the language of Greece.
2. In Scripture, a Gentile, as opposed to a Jew.
GREEK, a. Pertaining to Greece.
GRECIAN, n. A native of Greece; also, one versed in the Greek language.
The New Testament was originally written in Greek, the common tongue of the eastern empire.
scriptures: And there were certain Greeks among them that came up to worship at the feast:
Act 17:4
And some of them believed, and consorted with Paul and Silas; and of the devout Greeks a great multitude, and of the chief women not a few.
For the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom:
Gal 3:28
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Galatians 3:28 is lifted out of its argument and made to erase every distinction God has made, when Paul is settling one question only: who may be an heir.
corruption_paragraphs: “Neither Jew nor Greek… neither male nor female” has become the proof text for flattening every creational distinction, as though the verse dissolved sex, office, and calling together. Read the chapter and the point is exact. Paul is answering whether a Gentile must become a Jew to inherit Abraham's promise. His answer is that all who are Christ's are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise — equally, without qualification. The clause concerns standing in Christ and title to the inheritance. The same apostle who wrote it goes on in other letters to order the church by the very distinctions this verse is made to abolish, which is decisive: he did not think he had abolished them.

The recovery is to let the verse do its own enormous work. It is the death of every claim that grace runs along bloodlines, and it is the charter of the Gentile's full sonship. The Greek who once sought wisdom in the schools is now a son and an heir on precisely the same footing as the Jew who once trusted his circumcision — not because the difference between them was declared unreal, but because Christ was made a curse for both.
roots_summary: Greek Hellen (G1672), a Greek, a Gentile; Hellenistes (G1675), a Grecian Jew; sophia (G4678), wisdom.
roots_lines: Greek Hellen (G1672) — a Greek, and by extension a Gentile; John 12:20, Romans 1:16, 1 Corinthians 1:22.
Greek Hellenistes (G1675) — a Grecian, a Greek-speaking Jew; Acts 6:1, Acts 9:29.
Greek sophia (G4678) — wisdom, the thing the Greeks sought; 1 Corinthians 1:22-24.
Greek moria (G3472) — foolishness, the cross as the Greeks judged it; 1 Corinthians 1:23.
Greek ethnos (G1484) — nation, the wider term for the Gentiles; Matthew 28:19.
usage: “The Greeks seek after wisdom” — the national appetite Paul names and confounds.
“Certain Greeks… came up to worship” — the nations arriving before the Passion.
“Neither Jew nor Greek” — one title to the inheritance, in Christ.

pos: n. pl. (a nomadic people allied to Israel through Moses' father in law; Hebrew Qeni)
etymology: From a root associated with smiths or metalworkers, and with the nest (qen) — a pun Balaam turns on them when he sees their dwelling set in a rock.
biblical_def: The Kenites were a tent-dwelling people of the south, bound to Israel not by blood but by kindness. Moses' father in law was of them, and when Israel came up out of Egypt the Kenites shewed them kindness in the wilderness — a mercy God did not forget for four hundred years. The children of the Kenite went up with Judah into the wilderness south of Arad and dwelt among the people; Heber the Kenite severed himself from his kin and pitched his tent by Kedesh, and it was in his tent that Sisera died at Jael's hand. Balaam, looking on them from the heights, took up his parable: “Strong is thy dwellingplace, and thou puttest thy nest in a rock” (Num 24:21). Centuries later, when Saul was sent to destroy Amalek, he first warned the Kenites to depart, “for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel” (1Sa 15:6). The Rechabites, commended by Jeremiah for their obedience, are reckoned of this stock. They are Scripture's standing witness that the God of Israel keeps account of kindness done to His people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Kenite; the sense is fixed by the Hebrew text as a people of the south allied to Israel.
webster_full: The name is not in Webster's 1828 dictionary, which does not treat the Scripture gentilics.
KENITE. A people of Midianite stock, dwelling in the south of Canaan and in the wilderness of Judah.
The tribe of Moses' father in law, variously called Jethro, Reuel, and Hobab.
Their name is connected with the Hebrew for a smith, and by wordplay with qen, a nest.
The Rechabites of Jeremiah 35 are reckoned of the Kenites in 1 Chronicles 2:55.
scriptures: Jdg 1:16

And the children of the Kenite, Moses' father in law, went up out of the city of palm trees with the children of Judah into the wilderness of Judah, which lieth in the south of Arad; and they went and dwelt among the people.
Jdg 4:11
Now Heber the Kenite, which was of the children of Hobab the father in law of Moses, had severed himself from the Kenites, and pitched his tent unto the plain of Zaanaim, which is by Kedesh.
And he looked on the Kenites, and took up his parable, and said, Strong is thy dwellingplace, and thou puttest thy nest in a rock.

And Saul said unto the Kenites, Go, depart, get you down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them: for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel, when they came up out of Egypt. So the Kenites departed from among the Amalekites.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps a long account of kindness shewn to His people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Kenites are too obscure to be fought over, and the danger here is not distortion but neglect — a reader skims the gentilic and misses one of the plainest demonstrations in Scripture of how God remembers.

The principle to recover is the length of the divine memory. Four hundred years separate the kindness shewn in the wilderness from Saul's warning at the edge of the Amalekite slaughter, and the LORD had not forgotten it. Two nations stood side by side in the same country; one had met Israel with a sword and was marked for destruction, the other had met Israel with kindness and was told to depart in peace. The Kenites also show that nearness to the covenant people is a real mercy without being covenant membership: Jael acted for Israel, the Rechabites obeyed their father when Judah would not obey God, and Balaam saw their nest set in a rock. What a man does to the people of God is never lost, in either direction.
roots_summary: Hebrew Qeni (H7017), Kenite; qen (H7064), a nest; chesed (H2617), kindness, the word used of what they shewed Israel.
roots_lines: Hebrew Qeni (H7017) — a Kenite; Numbers 24:21, Judges 1:16, 1 Samuel 15:6.
Hebrew qen (H7064) — a nest; the wordplay in Balaam's parable, Numbers 24:21.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — kindness, covenant mercy; 1 Samuel 15:6.
Hebrew Chober (H2268) — Heber, the Kenite in whose tent Sisera fell; Judges 4:11.
1 Chronicles 2:55 reckons the house of Rechab among the Kenites.
usage: “Ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel” — a mercy remembered four centuries.
“Thou puttest thy nest in a rock” — Balaam's parable on their dwelling.
“They went and dwelt among the people” — a stranger folk settled inside Judah.

pos: n. (eldest son of Ham; also the land south of Egypt, rendered Ethiopia in the KJV; Hebrew Kush)
etymology: Hebrew Kush, the name of Ham's firstborn and of the territory his descendants held beyond the rivers of Egypt. The KJV usually translates the land as Ethiopia and keeps Cush for the man.
biblical_def: Cush is first a man and then a country. In the table of nations he stands first among the sons of Ham, father of Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabtecha — and, notoriously, of Nimrod, who “began to be a mighty one in the earth” (Gen 10:8) and built Babel. From that one line come both the tower of rebellion and the far southern nation that Scripture repeatedly holds up as the edge of the known world. Isaiah names Cush among the places from which the LORD will recover the remnant of His people the second time (Isa 11:11), setting it beside Assyria, Egypt, Elam, and Shinar in a list of the lands of dispersion. The prophets use the country as a measure of distance and of difference — can the Ethiopian change his skin? — and then overturn the measure with promise: from beyond the rivers of Ethiopia the suppliants shall bring an offering, and Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God. The Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah in his chariot is that promise arriving.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not enter Cush; the name is fixed by the Hebrew text as Ham's eldest son and the land of his posterity.
webster_full: The proper name is not entered in Webster's 1828 dictionary, which omits the Scripture gentilics.
CUSH. The eldest son of Ham, and the country peopled by his descendants.
ETHIOPIA, the term by which the Authorized Version usually renders the land of Cush.
The region lay south of Egypt, beyond the cataracts, and is described as beyond the rivers of Ethiopia.
From Cush descended Nimrod, the founder of Babel and the first named empire builder.
scriptures: Gen 10:6
And the sons of Ham; Cush, and Mizraim, and Phut, and Canaan.
Gen 10:7
And the sons of Cush; Seba, and Havilah, and Sabtah, and Raamah, and Sabtecha: and the sons of Raamah; Sheba, and Dedan.
Gen 10:8
And Cush begat Nimrod: he began to be a mighty one in the earth.

And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.
corruption_summary: Ham's line has been abused to prop a doctrine of cursed races, which the text of Genesis flatly refuses.
corruption_paragraphs: The name of Cush sits inside one of the most abused passages in Scripture. Noah's curse in Genesis 9 fell upon Canaan, not upon Ham and not upon Ham's other sons, and it was worked out in the dispossession of the Canaanite tribes before Israel. Cush is named in the very next chapter as Ham's firstborn and is never placed under that curse. Any reading that stretches the words over a whole branch of the human family is a fabrication laid on the text, and it collapses the moment the sentence is read as written. Scripture knows one blood of which God made all nations, one Adam fallen, one Christ raised.

The recovery is to follow what Scripture actually does with Cush, which is to make it the far horizon that the gospel reaches. The land beyond the rivers is named among the countries of the dispersion from which the remnant is recovered; from beyond those rivers the suppliants bring an offering; Ethiopia stretches out her hands unto God. Then Philip is sent down a desert road to one man from that country, reading the prophet, and the far horizon comes home. The line that produced Nimrod and Babel also receives, by grace, an early Gentile convert going on his way rejoicing.
roots_summary: Hebrew Kush (H3568), Cush; Kushi (H3569), a Cushite or Ethiopian; the KJV commonly renders the land as Ethiopia.
roots_lines: Hebrew Kush (H3568) — Cush, son of Ham and the land of his seed; Genesis 10:6, Isaiah 11:11.
Hebrew Kushi (H3569) — a Cushite, Ethiopian; Jeremiah 13:23, Jeremiah 38:7.
Hebrew Nimrod (H5248) — Nimrod, son of Cush, builder of Babel; Genesis 10:8-10.
Greek Aithiops (G128) — an Ethiopian; Acts 8:27.
The Authorized Version usually renders the land Ethiopia and reserves Cush for the man and a few place references.
usage: “And Cush begat Nimrod” — the line from which Babel came.
“From Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar” — the lands of the second recovery.
“The sons of Ham; Cush, and Mizraim” — first in the Hamite table of nations.

pos: n. (the Babylonian name given to Mishael, one of Daniel's three companions)
etymology: A Babylonian name imposed on a Hebrew captive. His given name Mishael meant ‘who is what God is?’ — and the new name, bound to a heathen deity, could not unmake the confession the old one carried.
biblical_def: Meshach is the name the prince of the eunuchs laid on Mishael, one of the four young men of Judah carried to Babylon with Daniel. The renaming was policy: strip the Hebrew name that confessed the LORD, fit the young man with a name honouring Babylon's gods, feed him the king's meat, teach him the Chaldean tongue, and in three years the captive is a courtier. It worked on everything except the man. When Nebuchadnezzar set up the golden image and the whole plain fell down at the sound of the music, Meshach stood with Shadrach and Abednego. Their answer to the king is one of the high points of Scripture: they were not careful to answer him in the matter, their God was able to deliver them, and He would deliver them — but if not, they would still not serve his gods nor worship the golden image. They were cast bound into a furnace heated sevenfold, and the king rose up astonished to see a fourth in the fire. Nebuchadnezzar himself pronounced the verdict: they had yielded their bodies rather than serve any god except their own God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not enter Meshach; the name is fixed by the book of Daniel as the Babylonian style of Mishael.
webster_full: The proper name is not entered in Webster's 1828 dictionary.
MESHACH. The Chaldee name given to Mishael, of the children of Judah, in the court of Nebuchadnezzar.
Daniel 1:7 records the renaming of all four young men on their entrance into the king's service.
Mishael signifies, Who is what God is?
With Shadrach and Abednego he was cast into the burning fiery furnace and delivered unhurt.
scriptures: Dan 1:7
Unto whom the prince of the eunuchs gave names: for he gave unto Daniel the name of Belteshazzar; and to Hananiah, of Shadrach; and to Mishael, of Meshach; and to Azariah, of Abednego.
Dan 3:16
Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, answered and said to the king, O Nebuchadnezzar, we are not careful to answer thee in this matter.
Dan 3:17
If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king.
Dan 3:28

Then Nebuchadnezzar spake, and said, Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who hath sent his angel, and delivered his servants that trusted in him, and have changed the king's word, and yielded their bodies, that they might not serve nor worship any god, except their own God.
corruption_summary: The furnace is retold as a promise that faith always spares the faithful, which is exactly the half these three refused to claim.
corruption_paragraphs: The story is commonly preached as a guarantee: trust God and the fire will not touch you. That reading has to cut the sentence in half. Meshach and his companions said their God was able to deliver, and that He would — and then added the words that make the confession worth anything at all: but if not, we will still not serve thy gods. They committed themselves before they knew the outcome, and they bound themselves to obedience in either case. Strip the second half away and the courage becomes a wager on a rescue, which is not faith but calculation.

The recovery is to preach both halves. God is able; that is not in doubt and never was. Whether He delivers in this instance is His to determine, and the believer's duty does not move with the answer. Hebrews sets the two side by side without embarrassment — some quenched the violence of fire, and others were tortured, not accepting deliverance. Meshach walked out of the furnace with not a hair singed; other saints have walked into fires they did not walk out of, and the same faith carried them. Nebuchadnezzar named the thing precisely: they yielded their bodies.
roots_summary: Aramaic Meyshak (H4335), Meshach; Hebrew Mishael (H4332), ‘who is what God is?’; Aramaic attun nura, the burning fiery furnace.
roots_lines: Aramaic Meyshak (H4335) — Meshach, the Babylonian name; Daniel 1:7, Daniel 3:16.
Hebrew Mishael (H4332) — Mishael, who is what God is?; Daniel 1:6-7.
Aramaic attun (H861) — a furnace; Daniel 3:6, Daniel 3:17.
Aramaic tselem (H6755) — the golden image set up in the plain of Dura; Daniel 3:1.
Hananiah became Shadrach and Azariah became Abednego in the same renaming.
usage: “We are not careful to answer thee in this matter” — no deliberation was required.
“But if not” — the clause that makes the confession faith and not a wager.
“Yielded their bodies” — Nebuchadnezzar's own account of what he had seen.

pos: n. (a prophetic name for Jerusalem in Isaiah 29; also a man among Ezra's chief men; Hebrew Ariel)
etymology: Hebrew Ariel, most naturally ‘lion of God’, but bearing also the sense ‘hearth of God’ or altar-hearth — the place where the fire burns and the sacrifice is consumed. Isaiah plays on both.
biblical_def: Ariel is the name Isaiah lays on Jerusalem in his ninth woe: “Woe to Ariel, to Ariel, the city where David dwelt!” (Isa 29:1). The city is identified past mistaking — David's city, keeping its round of feasts, adding year to year and killing sacrifices. The name is chosen for its double edge. Jerusalem is the lion of God, the strong city of the King; and Jerusalem is the altar-hearth, the place where victims burn. The LORD says He will distress Ariel, “and it shall be unto me as Ariel” (Isa 29:2) — the city that has been the hearth on which sacrifices are consumed will itself become the sacrifice on the hearth. The nations that fight against her are then swept away like a dream of a night vision, so that the same oracle carries both the burning and the deliverance. The name belongs also to a man: Ariel is listed among the chief men Ezra sent to Iddo to fetch ministers for the house of God (Ezr 8:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not enter Ariel as a Scripture name; the sense is fixed by Isaiah as a designation of Jerusalem.
webster_full: The Scripture name is not entered in Webster's 1828 dictionary.
ARIEL. A name given by Isaiah to Jerusalem, the city where David dwelt.
The Hebrew admits the sense, lion of God, and also, hearth or altar of God.
Ezekiel 43:15-16 uses a kindred form for the upper hearth of the altar.
Ariel is also the name of one of the chief men sent by Ezra to Casiphia.
scriptures: Isa 29:1
Woe to Ariel, to Ariel, the city where David dwelt! add ye year to year; let them kill sacrifices.
Isa 29:2
Yet I will distress Ariel, and there shall be heaviness and sorrow: and it shall be unto me as Ariel.
Isa 29:7
And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, even all that fight against her and her munition, and that distress her, shall be as a dream of a night vision.
Ezr 8:16

Then sent I for Eliezer, for Ariel, for Shemaiah, and for Elnathan, and for Jarib, and for Elnathan, and for Nathan, and for Zechariah, and for Meshullam, chief men; also for Joiarib, and for Elnathan, men of understanding.
corruption_summary: The name has been lifted out of Isaiah into occult and literary use as a spirit or airy familiar, which has nothing to do with the burning hearth of the prophet's woe.
corruption_paragraphs: Ariel is better known now from stage and story than from Isaiah — an airy spirit, a sprite, a name for something light and bodiless. That is a borrowing from literature and from the grimoires, not from Scripture, and it inverts the prophet's image completely. Isaiah's Ariel is not weightless; it is the heaviest thing in the chapter, a hearth heaped with sacrifice, a city under a woe, a place of fire and sorrow. Where the name has drifted into occult lists of spirits, the drift is worse than careless, for it hands a word God used to indict His own city over to the very traffic the same prophet condemns.

The recovery is to read the woe and feel the pun land. Jerusalem had kept the calendar impeccably — add ye year to year, let them kill sacrifices — while drawing near with the mouth and removing the heart far away. God's answer is to make the altar-city into the offering. The lion of God is brought low, and the deliverance, when it comes, comes as a gift and not as a wage. Every congregation that keeps a faultless calendar over a distant heart is standing where Ariel stood.
roots_summary: Hebrew Ariel (H740), lion of God, also altar-hearth; from ari (H738), lion, and El, God; compare harel in Ezekiel 43:15.
roots_lines: Hebrew Ariel (H740) — Ariel, a name for Jerusalem and of a man; Isaiah 29:1, Ezra 8:16.
Hebrew ari (H738) — a lion; the first element of the name.
Hebrew El (H410) — God, the second element of the name.
Hebrew harel / ariel (H2025) — the altar hearth; Ezekiel 43:15-16.
The doubled cry, “Woe to Ariel, to Ariel”, marks the ninth of Isaiah's woes.
usage: “Woe to Ariel… the city where David dwelt” — Jerusalem named past mistaking.
“It shall be unto me as Ariel” — the altar-city made the offering.
“As a dream of a night vision” — the besieging nations undone.

pos: n. (Ezekiel's name for Samaria, the elder of two harlot sisters; Hebrew Oholah)
etymology: Hebrew Oholah, ‘her own tent’ — a tent of her own making, over against her sister whose name confesses the LORD's tent in her. The northern kingdom set up its own sanctuary at Bethel and Dan.
biblical_def: Aholah is the name the LORD gives Samaria in Ezekiel's parable of the two sisters. Both were His; both bore sons and daughters; and the elder, Aholah, “played the harlot when she was mine” (Eze 23:5). Her name means her own tent, and the sense is exact: the northern kingdom raised a worship of its own devising, calves at Bethel and Dan, a priesthood of the lowest of the people, a feast in a month devised of its own heart. Ezekiel presses the figure without softening it. She doted on the Assyrians her neighbours, on captains and rulers and horsemen, and pursued the political alliances that always carried their gods with them. The judgment fits the sin: the LORD delivered her into the hand of the very lovers upon whom she doted (Eze 23:9), and the Assyrians who had been courted took her sons and daughters and slew her with the sword. She became famous among women — a byword, an object lesson standing in the record for her younger sister to read. Judah read it and did worse.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not enter Aholah; the name is fixed by Ezekiel 23 as the figure for Samaria.
webster_full: The proper name is not entered in Webster's 1828 dictionary.
AHOLAH. In Ezekiel 23, the elder of two sisters, expressly interpreted of Samaria.
The name signifies, her tent, or her own tabernacle.
Her sister Aholibah, my tent is in her, denotes Jerusalem.
She is charged with doting upon the Assyrians and was given into their hand.
scriptures: Eze 23:4
And the names of them were Aholah the elder, and Aholibah her sister: and they were mine, and they bare sons and daughters. Thus were their names; Samaria is Aholah, and Jerusalem Aholibah.
Eze 23:5
And Aholah played the harlot when she was mine; and she doted on her lovers, on the Assyrians her neighbours,
Eze 23:9
Wherefore I have delivered her into the hand of her lovers, into the hand of the Assyrians, upon whom she doted.
These discovered her nakedness: they took her sons and her daughters, and slew her with the sword: and she became famous among women; for they had executed judgment upon her.
corruption_summary: The chapter's deliberate coarseness is treated as an embarrassment to be edited, when God chose that language precisely so idolatry could not be discussed politely.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 23 is among the passages most often passed over in public reading, and where it is handled the instinct is to apologise for its bluntness. But the coarseness is the point and it is God's own choice of words. Idolatry among a covenant people is not a difference of opinion about worship; it is marital treachery, and the LORD insists on the vocabulary of adultery because every gentler term would let the offence be discussed at a comfortable distance. Aholah was not mistaken. She was His, and she went after others. To file the edges off the parable is to lose the exact thing it was given to convey.

The principle to recover is that the sin and its punishment are the same object seen twice. She doted on the Assyrians; she was given into the hand of the Assyrians. God's judgment here is not an arbitrary penalty attached to an offence but the offence granted its full wish. That is a mercy to anyone still able to read it, which is why the parable is addressed to the younger sister. Samaria's ruin stood in plain sight as Judah's warning, and Judah looked straight at it and was more corrupt than she.
roots_summary: Hebrew Oholah (H170), her tent; from ohel (H168), a tent or tabernacle; zanah (H2181), to play the harlot; agab (H5689), to dote.
roots_lines: Hebrew Oholah (H170) — Aholah, her own tent; Ezekiel 23:4-5.
Hebrew ohel (H168) — a tent, tabernacle; the root of both sisters' names.
Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit fornication, play the harlot; Ezekiel 23:5.
Hebrew agab (H5689) — to dote, to lust after; Ezekiel 23:5, Ezekiel 23:9.
The name contrasts with Aholibah, my tent is in her — Samaria's worship was of her own devising.
usage: “Samaria is Aholah” — the parable interpreted in the text itself.
“Played the harlot when she was mine” — the treachery is covenantal, not merely religious.
“Into the hand of her lovers” — the sin granted its wish as its sentence.

pos: n. (Ezekiel's name for Jerusalem, the younger of two harlot sisters; Hebrew Oholibah)
etymology: Hebrew Oholibah, ‘my tent is in her’ — the name confesses the very privilege that makes her sin the greater. Jerusalem had the true tabernacle, the ark, the temple, the priesthood.
biblical_def: Aholibah is the LORD's name for Jerusalem in Ezekiel's parable of the two sisters, and the name is an indictment before a word of charge is laid. Aholah, Samaria, means her own tent; Aholibah means my tent is in her. Judah had what the north never had — the house at Jerusalem, the ark, the ordained priesthood, the line of David, the prophets. She watched her elder sister court the Assyrians and be handed over to them, and then, Ezekiel says, “she was more corrupt in her inordinate love than she, and in her whoredoms more than her sister in her whoredoms” (Eze 23:11). She doted on Assyrians and then on Chaldeans, sending messengers into a far country after images she had seen portrayed upon a wall. The sentence follows the pattern of her sister's: “I will raise up thy lovers against thee” (Eze 23:22). The chapter closes by summoning the prophet to judge them both and declare their abominations, and by naming the end — they shall bear the sins of their idols, and shall know that He is the Lord GOD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not enter Aholibah; the name is fixed by Ezekiel 23 as the figure for Jerusalem.
webster_full: The proper name is not entered in Webster's 1828 dictionary.
AHOLIBAH. In Ezekiel 23, the younger of two sisters, expressly interpreted of Jerusalem.
The name signifies, my tent is in her, or my tabernacle is in her.
She is charged with exceeding her elder sister Aholah in corruption.
Her lovers, the Assyrians and Chaldeans, are raised up against her in judgment.
scriptures: And when her sister Aholibah saw this, she was more corrupt in her inordinate love than she, and in her whoredoms more than her sister in her whoredoms.
Therefore, O Aholibah, thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will raise up thy lovers against thee, from whom thy mind is alienated, and I will bring them against thee on every side;
The LORD said moreover unto me; Son of man, wilt thou judge Aholah and Aholibah? yea, declare unto them their abominations;
And they shall recompense your lewdness upon you, and ye shall bear the sins of your idols: and ye shall know that I am the Lord GOD.
corruption_summary: Privilege is assumed to be protection, when Ezekiel makes the indwelling tent the very thing that aggravates the guilt.
corruption_paragraphs: The standing assumption Aholibah embodies is that nearness to holy things is a safeguard. She had the temple, and Jeremiah heard the crowds chanting the temple of the LORD as if the building were a charm. Ezekiel destroys the assumption by putting it in her name. My tent is in her — and that is not her defence but the measure of her offence. She had seen exactly what became of Samaria, had the record of it, and went further. The sister who knew less sinned less. Light received raises the account rather than settling it.

The principle to recover presses hardest on those who have most. A church with sound confessions, a full shelf of doctrine, a faithful pulpit and a long memory is standing where Aholibah stood, and the possession of these things is not the same as fidelity in them. The end of the chapter is not despair but knowledge: they shall bear the sins of their idols, and they shall know that I am the Lord GOD. Judgment that ends in the knowledge of God is the severest mercy in the book, and it is offered before it is executed — which is why the prophet is told to declare their abominations to them.
roots_summary: Hebrew Oholibah (H172), my tent is in her; from ohel (H168), tent; taznuth (H8457), whoredom; toebah (H8441), abomination.
roots_lines: Hebrew Oholibah (H172) — Aholibah, my tent is in her; Ezekiel 23:4, Ezekiel 23:11.
Hebrew ohel (H168) — a tent, tabernacle; shared root with Aholah.
Hebrew taznuth (H8457) — whoredom, harlotry; Ezekiel 23:11.
Hebrew toebah (H8441) — abomination; Ezekiel 23:36.
Hebrew zimmah (H2154) — lewdness, a settled wicked purpose; Ezekiel 23:49.
usage: “Jerusalem Aholibah” — my tent is in her, and the name convicts.
“More corrupt… than her sister” — the one with more light went further.
“Ye shall know that I am the Lord GOD” — judgment ending in knowledge.

pos: n. (prince of Issachar in the wilderness; the KJV spelling of Nethanel, ‘God hath given’)
etymology: Hebrew Nethanel, from nathan, to give, and El, God — God hath given. The same elements, reversed and Graecised, yield Nathanael in the Gospel of John.
biblical_def: Nethaneel the son of Zuar is the prince of the tribe of Issachar during the wilderness years, named in the muster at Sinai, in the order of the camp, and in the twelve days of offerings at the dedication of the altar. His appearances are brief and almost entirely administrative — he is numbered, he is stationed, and on the second day he offers — yet the Holy Ghost has Moses record his charger and his bowl and his spoons at the same length as every other prince's, twelve times over, refusing to abbreviate. That refusal is the point of him. The name is borne by others in the record: a priest who blew a trumpet before the ark, a Levite scribe's father in the courses of the priests (1Ch 24:6), a musician, and men who returned from captivity. In every instance the name confesses the same thing — God hath given — and it is worth noticing that the men who carry it appear chiefly in lists, camps, courses, and rotas. The confession fits the setting: the giving is God's, and the service is ordinary and ordered.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) does not enter Nethaneel; the name is fixed by the Hebrew text as, God hath given.
webster_full: The proper name is not entered in Webster's 1828 dictionary.
NETHANEEL. The Authorized Version spelling of the Hebrew Nethanel, God hath given.
The son of Zuar, prince of the children of Issachar in the wilderness.
He offered on the second day at the dedication of the altar, Numbers 7:18-23.
The name is borne by several priests, Levites and musicians in the later histories.
scriptures: Num 1:8
Of Issachar; Nethaneel the son of Zuar.
Num 2:5
And those that do pitch next unto him shall be the tribe of Issachar: and Nethaneel the son of Zuar shall be captain of the children of Issachar.
Num 7:18
On the second day Nethaneel the son of Zuar, prince of Issachar, did offer:

And Shemaiah the son of Nethaneel the scribe, one of the Levites, wrote them before the king, and the princes, and Zadok the priest, and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar, and before the chief of the fathers of the priests and Levites: one principal household being taken for Eleazar, and one taken for Ithamar.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God records ordinary faithful service at full length.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nethaneel is too minor a figure to be contested. The real danger is the reader's own impatience, which skims the genealogies and the offering lists as filler on the way to the narrative.

The principle to recover is the dignity of the ordinary in God's reckoning. Numbers 7 is one of the longest chapters in the Bible, and its length comes entirely from repetition: twelve princes bring identical gifts, and the identical inventory is written out twelve separate times. It would have cost the writer three lines to say that each prince brought the same offering. God did not want it summarised. Nethaneel of Issachar is not distinguished from his brethren by anything he brought, and he is named, dated, and itemised anyway. That is how the LORD keeps books — the cup of cold water is remembered, the widow's two mites are counted, the labour of love shewn toward His name is not forgotten. Most Christian service is second-day service, indistinguishable from a brother's, and it is written down in full.

“Shall be captain of the children of Issachar” — his station in the camp.
